messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 78
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Roofer
- Trauma Type: Toxic chemical exposure
- Pcl5: 64

# A Roofer's Reckoning

Hassan has worked roofs for fifty-three years. His hands are weathered, mapped with calluses and old scars from decades of nails and tar and sun. He's proud of this—the physical evidence of a life spent building shelter for others. Even now, at seventy-eight, he still climbs ladders, though his knees protest and his wife, Amira, watches from below with worry etched into her face.

The incident happened three years ago on a commercial building downtown. Hassan was hired to repair the flat roof of an old warehouse that was being converted into apartments. It was late summer, brutally hot, and the job seemed routine—he'd done a thousand like it. But someone had stored industrial solvents in the building without proper documentation. When the contractors began demolition work inside, chemical fumes rose through the ventilation system and accumulated on the roof where Hassan was working.

He remembers the smell first—acrid, chemical, wrong—and then the burning in his eyes and throat. He remembers his vision blurring, his chest tightening as if someone had wrapped wire around his ribs. He tried to descend the ladder but his legs wouldn't cooperate properly. A younger worker found him sitting on the roof edge, gasping, confused about where he was. The ambulance ride, the hospital, the tests—it all blurs together now in his memory.

The physical recovery took months. His lungs cleared. His vision normalized. The doctors said he was lucky; exposure could have been much worse. But something didn't return to normal, and Hassan struggles to articulate what that something is.

Now, when he's on a roof, his heart races before he even reaches the top of the ladder. His palms sweat. Sometimes he can't catch his breath, and he has to sit down, gripping the edge, convinced he's dying. The smell of anything chemical—gasoline, paint thinner, even certain cleaning products—sends him spiraling. Last month, Amira used a new floor cleaner in the kitchen. Hassan smelled it, and suddenly he was back on that warehouse roof, gasping, unable to trust his own body.

He's had to turn down jobs. This is the part that eats at him most. A contractor he's worked with for thirty years called about a prestigious roofing project, and Hassan had to say no. He couldn't explain why to the man—how could he tell him that his body refuses to cooperate, that fear has become as much a part of him as his calluses?

The nightmares started about six months after the exposure. He wakes at three or four in the morning, drenched in sweat, his chest heaving. In the dreams, he can't breathe. The chemical smell is everywhere, suffocating, inescapable. Sometimes in the dreams he falls from the roof. Sometimes he's paralyzed, watching the fumes approach. Amira lies beside him, pretending to sleep, but he knows she's awake, listening to him suffer.

He's withdrawn from his men's group at the mosque. He doesn't want to explain. He doesn't want their pity or their questions. Instead, he sits in his garage workshop, organizing tools that don't need organizing, avoiding the roof work that once defined him. When he does climb a ladder now—and he still does, because stopping feels like dying—he moves slowly, checking and rechecking his footing, his mind screaming danger even when there is none.

Amira convinced him to come talk to someone. "You're not yourself," she said gently. Hassan isn't sure he knows who himself is anymore.
